title: Can Ethics Be Instilled into AI ? A Flourishing Ethics Approach
abstract: What ethical values and principles should guide and govern AI entities? This is just one of many AI‐related questions facing the world today. Another question—perhaps even more important—is Can ethical values and principles be instilled into AI entities to guide and govern them ? The present essay addresses the question of whether Flourishing Ethics is potentially a global ethical framework that prioritizes human flourishing while, at the same time, accommodating cultural diversity. It focuses upon possible use of LLMs to create moral advisers; and it is intended to support current worldwide efforts to keep AI developments within the bounds of universal ethical principles.

title: Phainesthai Formalised? Cogito, ergo ‘res’ sum in Conscious Agent Theory
abstract: The problem of consciousness remains the most intractable question in the philosophy of mind. Scientific approaches to consciousness, in their effort to provide a systematic account, impose determinate structures. This methodological necessity encounters a dilemma: it seeks to define what is never self‐identical. This paper considers Conscious Agent Theory (CAT) within this broader challenge, assessing its attempt to model consciousness while rejecting materialist reductionism. In rendering consciousness as a structured agent, CAT fortifies the problem by generating a fundamental tension between self‐transcendence and reification. Engaging with phenomenology and existentialist thought, the paper explores how being‐for‐itself resists reduction. The challenge from embodiment reveals that CAT risks erasing the transcendence distinguishing consciousness from the world it discloses, or reinstating dualism. CAT's tendency towards reification entails a Cartesian inheritance, placing it in opposition to phenomenological accounts of consciousness as relational, and self‐transcending. This dialectical tension invites further discussion between scientific perspectives and phenomenology.

title: The Systemic Unity of Philosophy Through Holism and Realism
abstract: Given the increasing specialization of contemporary philosophical inquiry, this paper asks whether philosophy can still be conceived as a unitary form of knowledge endowed with a fundamental function underlying its various branches. It argues that the essential nature of philosophy lies in thought's never‐ending metatheoretical self‐transcendence towards ever more comprehensive explanations and justifications. The paper defends this metaphilosophical conception by showing how it provides a coherent interpretation of epistemological and semantic holism within a realist ontological framework. Building primarily on Hilary Putnam's contribution to the contemporary debate on holism and realism, it develops this metatheoretical integration of metaphilosophy and epistemology from a pragmatic‐transcendental perspective. Philosophy thus emerges as an open and unitary system of mutually irreducible yet interconnected theoretical metastructures, preserving both the constitutive openness and the unity of knowledge as a whole.

title: Diagnosing Merely Verbal Disputes: A Case Study on Personal Identity
abstract: Merely verbal disputes have attracted considerable attention in metaphilosophy. Yet the critical task of discussing workable diagnostic methods for determining which disputes are merely verbal has been largely neglected, and detailed case studies of philosophical debates are rare. This paper addresses both of these gaps. In a first step, it introduces and discusses a diagnostic method for substantiating the serious possibility that a philosophical debate is merely verbal. In a second step, the paper applies this method in a novel case study of the personal identity debate. It argues that the method substantiates the serious possibility that the personal identity debate is merely verbal while also pointing to a potential, more fundamental disagreement that should be at the heart of this debate if the interpretation as a merely verbal dispute is misguided.

title: Capabilities, Human Nature, and Liberalism
abstract: This paper reconstructs and addresses three major critiques of Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach (CA): (1) the claim that an exclusive focus on capabilities (rather than functioning) is ineffective in protecting people's well‐being; (2) the critique of paternalism; and (3) the objection according to which the CA relies on a vague notion of human nature. It argues that, while Nussbaum's account has the inner resources to partially address the objections, incorporating John Stuart Mill's harm principle offers a more robust defense of the CA. The paper contends that this liberal principle provides a sound criterion for distinguishing the human capabilities that merit political protection from those that do not. Moreover, the principle also allows the CA to better address the critiques of paternalism and laissez‐faire. After presenting this defense, the paper analyzes how the adoption of Mill's principle should shape the CA's treatment of self‐harm.

title: Friendly Fire: Did Margaret Macdonald Contribute to Susan Stebbing's Exclusion from the History of Analytic Philosophy?
abstract: This paper presents the case of Margaret Macdonald's (1903–1956) posthumous treatment of Susan Stebbing (1885–1943). After Stebbing's death, Macdonald—her Ph.D. student and collaborator—wrote an early history of analytic philosophy in which Stebbing's work is credited to Bertrand Russell (specifically, her account of ‘directional analysis’). The paper argues that this case contains two important lessons for practitioners of the history of philosophy engaged in scholarship recovering the work of women in philosophy's history. First, that we should not expect any subject of historical scholarship to be morally infallible. And, second, that cases such as this emphasise the importance of social context when it comes to understanding marginalised figures in philosophy's history.

title: Continental Philosophy Is Indeed Rigorous!
abstract: Unless one reads widely, the analytic and Continental divide gives license for both sides to ignore the other. In doing so, judgments about the rigor and clarity of analytic philosophy pervade without challenge since analytic philosophical training is the most common form of philosophy in the English‐speaking world. This paper is addressed to the analytic philosophical community. To meet that challenge, it has formulated what is rigorous about the various methods of Continental philosophy and problematizes the analytic biases about rigor often held against Continental philosophy. It argues that the various methods of Continental philosophy provide an academic rigor that exceeds and is better than analytic philosophy. These are: phenomenological rigor, existential rigor, hermeneutic rigor, and genealogical or deconstructionist rigor. In following these methods, it can be argued that Continental philosophy is indeed rigorous!

title: Metaphysics Reimagined
abstract: Metaphysics was dismissed in the 1920s and 1930s by Humeans (Ayer) and formalist Kantians (Carnap) for its verbiage and speculation. Heidegger and Hegel were plausible targets. Renewal is thwarted because we lack accord about the meaning of its name. Current versions are allusive, philosophy at the frontier of mysticism or piety. Others emphasize inspectable or inferred aspects of experience: percepts or their organization, mind's activity, or the language making it intelligible. These are derivatives of Plato's belief that awareness—the conscious reading of perceptual or rational content—is the window to reality; nothing, they imply, is better known to mind than mind itself. Practical life and science are alternative points of access. They address circumstances from the perspective of material needs or interests, then more systematically as testable inquiry. Darwin's account of evolution is evidence that the perceptions on which they're based accurately represent circumstances to a significant degree: we wouldn't exist to adapt and reproduce if they didn't. Categorial form was Aristotle's idea; his map of reality is the one elaborated and revised. Progress is slow, but real; we distinguish observation and testable hypotheses from allusive stories, fads, and metaphors.

title: The Self‐as‐Philosopher: A Schema‐Informed Reading of Philosophy as a Way of Life
abstract: This article offers an original reading of the process and outcomes of training in philosophy as a way of life. By drawing on research and theory from the fields of cognitive psychology and adult learning, it argues that the transformative effects frequently ascribed to the practice of philosophy as a way of life can helpfully be conceptualised in terms of schema change, and the development of a new philosophical self or identity in the student of philosophy. While the shifts in personality and worldview believed to follow from practising philosophy as a way of life have been described both in the ancient texts and in contemporary scholarship, the article suggests that this schema‐informed reading helps answer important questions regarding the transformative effects of philosophy, and also offers great promise to contemporary practitioners and researchers in the field of philosophy as a way of life.

title: Philosophical Microhistory: Its Nature, Scope, Value, and Challenges
abstract: This article elaborates and defends philosophical microhistory—the intensive study of small episodes such as quotes, marginal anecdotes, editorial decisions, or forgotten glosses—as an undertheorised approach to the historiography of philosophy. Adapting Italian microhistory, it treats ideas as semantic capital circulating through networks of thinkers, translators, and institutions. The article presents a framework centred on levels of abstraction, showing how microscopic and macroscopic scales function as complementary perspectives. It contextualises philosophical microhistory relative to Lovejoy's history of ideas, rational reconstruction, Cambridge contextualism, Begriffsgeschichte , reception history, and Foucauldian genealogy, arguing that the approach supplements rather than supplants existing methods. It addresses objections concerning antiquarianism, representativeness, and the micro–macro problem, concluding that digital humanities and global intellectual history present new opportunities. Philosophical microhistory emerges as a methodology valuing contingency, foregrounding marginal voices, and disclosing how philosophy's most significant topics may sometimes be shaped by its most minor details.

title: Philosophical Inquiry and Controversial Views
abstract: Should philosophers explore or engage with controversial and harmful views? This paper argues that this question can benefit from the literature on open‐mindedness in virtue epistemology and moral psychology. In particular, it shows that framing the question in terms of open‐mindedness is apt because open‐mindedness's dual nature as both an intellectual and a moral virtue makes it an especially appropriate and valuable tool for addressing a debate that is concerned with the potential moral harms of philosophical inquiry . Such a framing, the paper contends, is also fruitful because the literature on open‐mindedness contains important insights that are germane to the question of whether philosophers should inquire into harmful views, including considerations revolving around expertise and the mitigation of epistemic and moral danger, division of cognitive labor, and appropriate conditions for inquiry.

title: A Tale Signifying Much: How Shakespeare's Macbeth Teaches the Lessons of Plato's Republic , and Why Poetry and Philosophy Are Natural Allies
abstract: In Plato's Republic , Socrates' account of an ancient quarrel between poetry and philosophy closely concerns the failure of poets to defend justice as good in itself and not merely for its external benefits. No less an exemplum of poetry than Shakespeare's Macbeth does just that. Through a side‐by‐side comparison of the two texts, this paper shows that they both ask whether a life of injustice would make people happier if they could keep their unjust deeds hidden; both answer that it would not , relying on the role of thumos , the spirited part of the soul; and both give the additional answer that it is not possible to keep an unjust character hidden, for it eventually becomes evident to human beings and is never hidden to gods (or God). Without delineating the precise boundaries either of poetry or of philosophy, this shows that the ancient quarrel is resolvable and that philosophy and poetry make natural allies.

title: From “No Sense of Place” to “No Sense of the World”: Screen‐Centered Senses and the Problem of Worldlessness
abstract: Drawing on Heidegger and postphenomenology, this article examines how digital screens reshape human senses of place and world. Screens act as “focal devices” that structure daily perception, behavior, and lifestyle by capturing attention. Extending Meyrowitz, the article argues that screens induce not only placelessness but also worldlessness. The analysis distinguishes screen‐mediated from screen‐centered sense, where the latter traps perception within a closed loop, ultimately producing worldlessness. The tragic case of a young girl named Huang Yuanxin is analyzed to demonstrate the multidimensional manifestations of placelessness and worldlessness. Finally, invoking Heidegger and Arendt, the article demonstrates that screen‐induced worldlessness primarily erodes common sensibility ( sensus communis ). This erosion obscures and dissolves the public sphere, which relies on shared experience and discourse, as pervasive screens fragment it into isolated private realms.
